chapters.title: Tablet I
paragraphs: He is the one who has seen the story of Gilgamesh, who knows everything that happened to him, and who has seen every kind of wisdom. He knows the mysteries and has seen what lies hidden. He brings news from before the flood. He has traveled far-off roads and grown weary on them, and now he has set down all the rest on a memorial tablet. The wall of Uruk-supuru.
Two parts of him are god, and one part is human.
He spoke a charm that never leaves him, and then there is the god who, from days long past, —

His cattle deserted him. He went down to the river, pushed his boat out onto the water, and covered it over. Full of sorrow, he wept bitterly. Then he went back to the city of Gan-gan-na, which the enemy had utterly destroyed.

Mother donkeys trample their own foals, and cows in a frenzy turn on their calves. The cattle were terrified, and so were the people. The young women moan and grieve like doves. The gods of mighty-walled Erech take the shape of flies and buzz through the streets, and its guardian spirits become mice that scurry into their holes.

For three years the enemy laid siege to Erech. The city gates stayed shut and the bolts stayed fast, and even the goddess Ishtar could not stand against the enemy. Then Bel began to speak. He turned to Ishtar, the queen, and said to her:

chapters.title: Tablet II
paragraphs: Gilgamesh leaves no son with his father, no girl for her warrior, no wife for her husband. Their wailing and mourning can be heard everywhere.

"You gods of heaven, and you, Bel of Erech, who brought my son into being, save us! Gilgamesh has no rival in all the land. Your people have come to you for help. Gilgamesh leaves no child with its father." Day and night they poured out their complaint:

"He is the ruler of mighty-walled Erech. He is their ruler, the strong one, the exalted one, the cunning one. Gilgamesh does not leave a daughter with her mother, or a girl for her warrior, or a wife for her husband."

The gods of heaven heard their cry. They called out to the goddess Aruru: "Aruru, you made him. Now make a rival for him, for the day when his heart is stirred. Let the two of them fight, and let Erech look on!"

When Aruru heard this, she shaped in her mind a man in the image of the god Anu. She washed her hands, pinched off a bit of clay, and dropped it to the earth. And so she made Enkidu, the hero, a towering creature, the property of the god Ninib.

Hair covered his whole body, and the hair on his head was long, like a woman's, and thick and flowing like the grain-god's. Against the custom of the people and the land, he wore clothing, like the god Ner. He ate grass with the gazelles, drank with the animals, and played among the creatures of the water.

Sa-a-a-du, the hunter of men, lay in wait for him at the opening of the watering place. On the first day, the second, and the third, he lay in wait for him there. But when he saw him, the hunter's face turned troubled, and he went back to his house.
He was sad. He groaned and cried out. His heart grew heavy and his face darkened, and sorrow entered his mind. His face was like the face of one who has come a long way.

The hunter spoke to his father: "Father, one man who goes there is not strong enough. His strength is like that of a Kisir of Anu. He roams across all the mountains and feeds with the wild animals. Again and again his feet are set toward the watering place.

I am afraid of him, and I do not dare go near. He has filled in the pit I dug and torn up the nets I had spread. He has let the cattle and the wild animals slip out of my hands, and he will not let me hunt them."
His father opened his mouth and spoke to the hunter: "Go and make your way to Erech, the city of Gilgamesh.

Gilgamesh told the hunter: "Go, my hunter, and bring the temptress Uchat along. As soon as the animals head down to the water, let her pull off her dress and show herself. Enkidu will notice her and walk over to her, and the cattle that gather around him in the field will leave him."

The hunter set out and took the woman Uchat with him. They went straight on, and on the third day they reached the place. There the hunter and the temptress settled in their hiding spot. For one day and then a second they lay in wait at the entrance to the watering place, where the cattle came to drink and the water creatures played.

Then Enkidu came, he whose home was in the mountains, who ate grass with the gazelles, drank with the cattle, and delighted his heart among the creatures of the water. And Uchat, who lures men, looked at him.

"Look, there he is," the hunter said. "Now bare yourself, show your body, and let him take his pleasure of you. Do not be ashamed; give in to his desire. He will notice you and walk over to you. Pull off your robe so that he can lie in your arms. Satisfy him as a woman satisfies a man, and then the cattle that grew up beside him in the field will forsake him while he presses his chest firmly to yours."

Uchat did as she was told. She uncovered herself and let him have his pleasure. She was not ashamed but gave in to his desire. She took off her robe, he lay in her arms, and she satisfied him as a woman does. He pressed his chest firmly against hers. For six days and seven nights Enkidu enjoyed Uchat's love.

When he had had his fill of her, he turned his face back toward his herd. The gazelles lying at rest saw Enkidu, and they and the cattle of the field turned away from him. This shocked Enkidu. His body went weak and his knees stiffened as his animals moved off, and he was slower than he had ever been.

But as he listened, he came to a decision. Held fast by love, he turned back to the harlot's feet and gazed up into the temptress's face. His ears were fixed on her as she spoke, and she said to him: "You are noble, Enkidu, godlike. Why do you sleep among the wild beasts of the field? Come along and I will lead you to Erech with its strong walls, to the splendid house where Anu and Ishtar dwell, to Gilgamesh's palace, where lives that hero of flawless strength, who rises over other men in might like a wild bull."

As she spoke, he took her wise words to heart, and his heart longed for a friend. Enkidu answered the temptress: "Come then, Uchat, guide me to that splendid dwelling, the holy seat of Anu and Ishtar, to the palace of Gilgamesh, the hero of perfect strength, who stands above other men in power like a wild bull."

"Gilgamesh will see you. I can make out his face, and it glows with a hero's courage. He has strength, and his whole body is magnificent. His power is greater than yours. By day and by night he never rests or tires. Enkidu, change your plan. Shamash loves Gilgamesh, and Anu, Bel, and Ea breathe wisdom into his ear. Even before you descended from the mountain, Gilgamesh had seen you in a dream in Erech."
Gilgamesh came to understand the dream, and he said to his mother: "Mother, I had a dream in my vision of the night. The stars of heaven, like the host of Anu, fell down upon me."

Gilgamesh set out to learn what his dream meant, and he said to his mother: "Mother, in the course of my night I grew strong and walked among the heroes. Then from the starry sky a mass from the heavens fell on me. I lifted it, and it grew heavy on me. I became weak and could not bear its weight. The whole land of Erech gathered around it, and the heroes kissed its feet. It was lifted up in front of me, and they stood me back on my feet. I picked it up and carried it to you."

The mother of Gilgamesh, who knows everything, answered her son: "A man will come, Gilgamesh, born as you were in the open country and raised by the mountain. When you see him, you will be glad as a man is glad at the sight of a woman. Heroes will bend to kiss his feet. You will spare his life and work to bring him to me."

He slept and saw another dream, and he told it to his mother: "Mother, I have seen another dream. I saw my own likeness in the streets of broad Erech. An axe was being swung, and a crowd had gathered around the man. The axe angered him. I saw him and was glad. I loved him like a woman and embraced him, and I took him and treated him as my brother."
Gilgamesh's mother, who knows all things, told her son: "The man you saw, the one you took in your arms as one holds a woman, is a sign that he will be bound to you." Gilgamesh understood the dream.

Enkidu sat in front of the woman. He took her in his arms and lay with her, and he lost all memory of the land of his birth. For six days and seven nights Enkidu went on lying with the courtesan. Then the woman spoke to him: "I am looking at you, Enkidu, and you are godlike! Why do you roam the field with the cattle?

Come, let me lead you into Erech of the broad squares, to the holy house, the home of Anu. Rise, Enkidu, and let me take you to Eanna, where Anu lives, the place where Gilgamesh is, perfect in vigor. You will hold him as a wife is held and love him as you love yourself. Come, get up from this cursed ground."

He took in what she said and agreed to it. The woman's counsel sank into his heart. She took off one of her garments and put it on him, and kept another garment for herself. Taking him by the hand, she brought him, godlike, to the lush meadow and the sheepfolds. There they were given food.

He had been used to sucking the milk of the cattle. When they set food in front of him, he broke off a piece, looked at it, and stared. Enkidu did not know how to eat bread, and no one had taught him to drink wine. The woman spoke to him: "Eat the bread, Enkidu! It is what keeps us alive. Drink the wine, as the people of the land do!"

Enkidu ate until he was full. He drank wine, seven cups of it. His spirit loosened and he grew merry. His heart was glad and his face shone. A barber shaved the hair from his body, and he was rubbed with oil. He became like a man. He put on clothes and looked like a man.

He took up a weapon and went after lions, so that the night shepherds could rest. He drove in the dagger and beat the lions. The senior shepherds lay down to sleep, for Enkidu was their guard, the strong man, the one-of-a-kind hero. He speaks to the shepherds:

They were making merry. Enkidu lifted his eyes and saw a man. He spoke to the courtesan: "Courtesan, bring that man over. Why has he come to me? I will wipe out his name." The woman called to the man, and he came toward Enkidu and looked at him. "Go away! Why do you tremble? Your way of life is bad."

Then the man spoke to Enkidu: "To have a home and family is the destiny of men and the right of the noble. Load the work baskets for the city! Set aside food supplies for the city! For the king of Erech of the broad squares, open the bridal chamber and perform the wedding rite! For Gilgamesh, the king of Erech of the broad squares, open the bridal chamber and perform the wedding rite! One should lie with the lawful wife. So it was before, and so it will be after. By the decree of a god, from the cutting of his cord, this is his fate." At the hero's speech, Enkidu's face grew pale.

Enkidu went in front, and the courtesan followed behind him. He entered Erech of the broad squares, and the people crowded around him. As he stood in the street of Erech of the broad squares, the men gathered and said of him: "He has suddenly taken on the shape of Gilgamesh, only shorter in height. He is tall in build and powerful. He has become strong in the land. He used to suck the milk of cattle."

In Erech, day after day, the heroes rejoiced. Enkidu became a leader, a rival to the handsome hero, to Gilgamesh, who was like a god. A bed was spread for the goddess Ishhara. Gilgamesh lay down, and then, in the dark, he slipped away. He drew near, and Enkidu stood in the street and blocked Gilgamesh's path, showing his power.

Enkidu went out against him, his hair thick. He started toward him, and they met in the square of the district. Enkidu blocked the gate with his foot and would not let Gilgamesh come in. They grabbed each other and fought like bulls. They smashed the doorpost and cracked the wall. Gilgamesh and Enkidu grabbed each other and fought like bulls. They smashed the doorpost and cracked the wall. Gilgamesh was thrown, his foot bent to the ground. His anger passed and his chest grew calm.

When his chest was calm, Enkidu spoke to Gilgamesh: "Your mother bore you as one of a kind, Gilgamesh. Ninsun, the wild cow of the pen, has lifted your head high above other men, and Enlil has set kingship over the people as your portion."

chapters.title: Tablet III
paragraphs: The gods let you enter. Forsaken was the place, and the consort was there. And he saw it all alone, and he eased his heart and then spoke to his friend about it.

I had a dream in my sleep at night. The stars of heaven fell down upon the earth, and I stood there frightened. His face was disturbed. His nails were like the claws of a lion. The dream made me strong.

"Come. He will let you recline on a grand and splendid couch. He will place you on a couch, in the seat of honor at his left. The kings of the earth will bow and kiss your feet, and the people of Erech will cry out in front of you. The nations will work for you. Whatever there is will be carried along behind you, and in the middle of it he will pitch his camp."
Enkidu heard what Shamash, the warrior-hero, had said, and then his furious heart grew calm.

Tears filled Enkidu's eyes. He clutched at his heart and sighed in sorrow. Tears filled his eyes; he clutched at his heart and sighed in sorrow. Gilgamesh's face was grieved, and he spoke to Enkidu: "My friend, why do your eyes fill with tears? Why do you clutch at your heart and sigh so sadly?"
Enkidu answered Gilgamesh: "Assaults, my friend, have drained my strength. My arms hang limp, and my strength has grown weak." Then Gilgamesh replied to Enkidu:

Enkidu answered Gilgamesh: "Understand this, my friend. Up in the mountains, when I wandered with the cattle, I went a double hour's walk into the middle of the forest. Alone I pushed deep inside, to Huwawa, whose roar is a flood, whose mouth is fire, and whose breath is death. What makes you want to do this? Why head for the lair of Huwawa?"

Enkidu answered Gilgamesh: "When we go down together into the cedar forest, its guardian, Gilgamesh the warrior, is a tireless power: Huwawa, a child of Adad. To keep the cedar forest safe, Enlil has decreed a sevenfold terror for it."

Gilgamesh answered Enkidu: "My friend, whoever overcomes terror does well with Shamash for the length of his days. People will speak of it at the city gates. Wherever there is terror to face, you, it seems, are afraid to die. Your valor lacks strength. I will walk in front of you, even if your mouth calls out to me, 'You are afraid to come near.' If I fall, I will have made my name.

When you call out to me, you trouble my heart. I am determined to enter the cedar forest. I will truly make my name. The work, my friend, I will hand to the craftsmen. Let them cast weapons in front of us."

chapters.title: Tablet IV
paragraphs: We looked after you, O king of the gods. Now look after us as well.
To the lofty palace of the great queen, who knows everything.

He burned a smoke offering before Shamash and poured out a drink offering, and he lifted his hand to Shamash in prayer: "Why have you unsettled the heart of Gilgamesh? Now that you have instructed him, he travels a long road toward Humbaba. He is about to enter a battle he knows nothing about and to set out on a war he knows nothing about. From the day he sets out until the day he comes back, until he reaches the splendid cedar forest and has killed the tyrant Humbaba, every one of the many evils that meet him will wear him down. On the day when you —"
The forces of the land gathered together. The army finished its preparations, and the heroes put on their armor.

So that the cedar wood would stay untouched, Bel made it a terror to people. Humbaba's roaring was like a storm whirling across the land. His mouth was full of blasphemy, and his breath was like a scorching wind. Someone hears a roaring in the forest, whoever goes down into his park. So that the cedar forest would stay untouched, Bel made it a terror to people. Whoever enters it will be struck down by plague.

At every twenty double leagues they stopped for a meal, and at every thirty they stopped to rest. In front of Shamash they dug a hole. Then Gilgamesh climbed up and poured his offering of meal into the hole, saying: "Mountain, bring Enkidu a dream! Let him see visions in his sleep, O Shamash."

"My friend, did you call me? The dream I had was terrible. Heaven thundered and the earth shook. The day turned dark and darkness rose. Lightning struck and fire blazed up, glutted with destruction and filled with death. Then suddenly the light went dim and the fire was put out. It fell down and turned to smoke."

They gave the work to the smiths and assigned the workmen a place to live. The master smiths cast hatchets. They cast axes weighing three talents apiece. The master smiths cast lances, with blades of two talents each, and a spear of thirty minas fixed to each. The hilts of the lances, thirty minas of gold, went with them. Gilgamesh and Enkidu were each armed with ten talents' worth of weapons.

Enkidu sat in front of him, and thus he spoke: "Gilgamesh, of whom they speak, let me see him! His name fills the lands. I will lure him to the cedar forest, like a strong child of Erech. I will let the land hear that I am set on luring him into the cedar forest. I will make a name."

The elders of Erech of the broad squares sent word to Gilgamesh: "You are young, Gilgamesh, and your heart sweeps you off. You have no idea what you are proposing. We have heard that Huwawa is furious. Who has ever faced his weapon? Who has ever gone a double hour deep into that forest? Huwawa's roar is a deluge, fire comes from his mouth, and death is his breath. What makes you want to do this? Why walk toward the lair of Huwawa?"

Gilgamesh listened to what his advisers had reported. He looked up and called to his friend: "Now, my friend, here is what I say. I am afraid of him, but I will go to the cedar forest. I will make the journey beside you into the cedar forest.

At the rampart of Erech of the broad squares, Gilgamesh knelt before Shamash and spoke to him: "I will go, Shamash. I take hold of your hands. When I have saved my life, bring me back to the rampart in Erech. Grant me protection!"

"I am Gilgamesh, the mighty man of this country, and I set out on a road I have never traveled. If I succeed, I will praise you with a glad heart and celebrate the supremacy of your power. I will set you on thrones." The master smiths brought the weapons. They put the bow and quiver in his hands, and he took up the hatchet.

They took the road, his lance in his belt. Again they came up to Gilgamesh! "How long until you return to Erech?" Again the elders approached him and advised him about the journey: "Do not rely on your own strength, Gilgamesh! Gather provisions and protect yourself! Let Enkidu walk in front of you. He knows the way and has walked the road to the forest's entrance.

The one who goes ahead will save his companion. Provide for his road and protect yourself! May Shamash carry out your purpose! May he let your eyes see what your mouth has foretold. May he trace out the closed path for you! May he level the road for your steps! May he level the mountain for your feet! In your night, may Lugal-banda bring you a word that will make you glad, and stand by you in your purpose! Like a young man, may he make your purpose succeed!

In the river of Huwawa, as you plan, wash your feet! Dig a well all around you! May you always have pure water for your libation. Pour goblets of water out to Shamash! May Lugal-banda take note of it!"
Enkidu replied to Gilgamesh: "Since you are set on taking the road, do not let your heart fear. Rely on me! Put his dwelling into my hand!" On the road to Huwawa they went forward.

chapters.title: Tablet V
paragraphs: There they stood. The forest rose high above them, and they gazed in amazement at the height of the cedars and at the entrance to the cedar wood, where Humbaba used to walk with long strides. Roads were laid out and paths were well kept. They saw the cedar hill, the home of the gods, the sanctuary of Irnini. In front of the hill stood a cedar of great beauty. Its shade was fine and good, and it filled the heart with gladness.
The corpse, to be eaten by the vultures.

chapters.title: Tablet VI
paragraphs: He cleaned his weapons and burnished his arms. He stripped off the armor he had worn, laid aside his soiled clothes, and put on clean garments. He decked himself in his finery and set his headband in place. Gilgamesh placed the crown upon his head.

Ishtar, the lofty goddess, set her heart on winning the favor and love of Gilgamesh, and she said to him: "Come, Gilgamesh, take me as your spouse. Give me, oh give me, your manly vigor. Become my husband, and I will be your bride. I will seat you in a chariot adorned with precious stones and gold, its wheels of gold and its shafts of sapphire. You will yoke great kudanu-lions to it.

You will drive into our house beneath fragrant cedars. When you enter our house, you will sit on a high throne, and folk will kiss your feet; kings, lords, and princes will bend low before you. All that the mountains and the land produce they will bring you as tribute. Your ewes will bear twin lambs. They will bring mules as tribute. Your majesty will ride in a magnificent chariot, drawn by a team that has no equal."

But Gilgamesh opened his mouth and answered the lofty goddess Ishtar: "Where is your husband Tammuz, who was meant to live forever? And what has become of the allallu-bird? I will tell you plainly where your flirtations lead. To Tammuz, the husband of your youth, you brought weeping, and you bring grief on him every year.

You loved the allallu-bird, so bright in color, and then you broke and crushed its wing, so that now it sits in the woods and cries, 'My wing, my wing!' You loved a lion of perfect strength, and seven times and seven again you dug a trapping pit for him. You loved a horse, unrivaled in battle, and with bridle, spur, and whip you drove it on, forcing it to run seven double leagues without stopping. When it was worn out and wanted a drink, you still drove it on, and so you brought weeping and grief to its mother Si-li-li.

You loved a shepherd of the flock, too, who kept burning incense in front of you and slaughtered lambs for your pleasure day after day. You struck him and changed him into a tiger, so that his own young herdsmen chased him off and his own dogs tore him apart.

You loved a farmer, too, a gardener in your father's service, who kept bringing you delicacies and every day loaded your table. You cast your eye on him and turned his head, saying: "My farm boy, let us have a taste of your manly vigor. Put out your hand and take my virginity." But the farmer answered you: "Me! What is this you ask of me? Mother, you have not baked, and I will not eat. The food I would eat is foul and bitter, and it is covered with cold and numbness."

When you heard what he said, you hit him and transformed him into a cripple, and so forced him to lie on a couch, never able to get up from his bed. Now you want to love me as well, but I would fare like the rest of them."

When Ishtar heard these words, she was seized by rage. She rose up to heaven and came before her father Anu, and went to her mother Antum, and said to them: "Father, Gilgamesh has insulted me. Gilgamesh has reproached me for my evil deeds, deeds of evil and violence."

Anu opened his mouth and spoke to the mighty goddess Ishtar: "You need not stay so troubled, though Gilgamesh has reproached you for your evil deeds, deeds of evil and violence." Then Ishtar opened her mouth and spoke to her father Anu: "Father, make me a bull of heaven."
They hunted the bull, and Enkidu attacked the bull of heaven and seized it by its heavy tail.

Then Ishtar climbed up on the wall of mighty Erech. She shrieked and burst out in a curse: "Woe to Gilgamesh, who has grieved me like this and killed the bull of heaven." But Enkidu heard these words of Ishtar's, ripped off the right side of the bull of heaven, and hurled it into her face, saying: "I will beat you the same way, and I will do to you what I did to him. I will hang its heart upon your side."

Then Ishtar summoned her followers, the temple women who ruin men, the hierodules and the sacred prostitutes. She wept and wailed over the right side of the bull of heaven. But Gilgamesh called the people together, and all his craftsmen. The craftsmen marveled at the size of the horns. Their worth was thirty minas of precious stone, and they were as thick as a finger joint. Together they could hold six measures of oil.

He dedicated the horns for the anointing of his god Lugal-tur-da. He carried them in and hung them in the shrine of his lord. Then they washed their hands in the river Euphrates, took the road, set out for the city, and rode through the streets of Erech. The people of Erech gathered and stared in amazement.

Then Gilgamesh addressed the household servants of his palace and cried out to them: "Who is magnificent among the heroes? Who stands out among the men?" "Gilgamesh is magnificent among the heroes, Gilgamesh stands out among the men!"

Gilgamesh held a joyful feast in his palace. Then the heroes slept, stretched out on their couches. Enkidu slept too, and he saw a vision in his sleep. In the morning he got up and worked out the meaning of the dream, and he said to Gilgamesh: "My friend, why have the great gods held counsel?"

chapters.title: Tablet VII
paragraphs: "My friend, I saw a dream in the night. Heaven thundered and the earth answered. I stood before a mighty one, and his face was grim."

"It has brought me back, like a bird of darkness. I went down to the house of darkness, the home of the goddess Irkalla, to the house whose visitor never leaves, to the road whose way never turns back, to the house whose dwellers are robbed of light, to the place where dust is their sustenance and clay their food. They are dressed like birds, in garments of feathers. They see no light but sit in darkness.

In the house I have entered, my friend, crowns lie thrown down on the ground, and there live those who once wore crowns, who in days of old ruled countries, to whom Anu and Belit gave roasted meat to eat. Now cold meals are set out for them, and water from leather skins is poured out.

In the house I have entered, my friend, priests and ministers also live. Soothsayers and enchanters live there, and the temple anointers of the great gods. Etana lives there, and Ner. The queen of the earth lives there too, the goddess Ereshkigal. The scribe of the earth kneels before her and reads aloud in front of her, and Ereshkigal raised her head and saw me."

chapters.title: Tablet VIII
paragraphs: There is no other tree like you. Your height is six gar, and your thickness is two.
"I went out in good health, my friend. But the dream I dreamed has come true."

And Enkidu lay ill for twelve days. On the first day and the second, he lay sick on his couch. Then the third and the fourth, and the fifth, sixth, seventh, eighth, and on through the days, Enkidu lay sick on his couch. The eleventh day, the twelfth day, Enkidu still lay on his couch. Then he called out to Gilgamesh.

"Enkidu, my young friend, tiger of the wilderness, we have done everything we could and climbed the mountain. We seized the bull of heaven and killed it. We put Humbaba to death, the one who dwelt in the cedar forest. Now what is this sleep that has gripped you? You are dark and still, and you do not listen to me."

But Enkidu did not lift his eyes. Gilgamesh touched his heart, and it beat no more. Then he covered his friend like a bride. He cried out like a lion, like a lioness robbed of her cubs. He turned away.

chapters.title: Tablet IX
paragraphs: Gilgamesh wept bitterly over the death of Enkidu, his friend, and sprawled on the ground, saying: "I will not die the way Enkidu did. But grief has entered my heart, and fear of death has come over me, so I lie here stretched out on the ground. I will set out to test the strength of Per-napishtim, the son of Kidin-Marduk, and I will go right now."

"I reached a mountain pass at night. I saw lions and was frightened. But I raised my head and prayed to the god Sin. My cry came to the great majesty of the god; he listened and rescued me, me of all people."

In the night he saw a vision and a dream, and lions were frolicking. Raising the axe he held, he drew the sword from his belt. He threw himself in among them like a javelin, and he struck them, killed them, and scattered them.

He came to Mount Mashu, whose gate is watched every day by monsters, whose back reaches the dam of heaven, and whose chest reaches down to Aralu. Scorpion-men guard its gate. They spread dreadful terror, and to look at them is death. Their splendor is fearsome, strong enough to topple mountains. From sunrise until sunset they keep watch over the sun. Gilgamesh saw them, and his face went dark with fear and dread. His mind was thrown into confusion by their wild appearance.

Then one scorpion-man said to his wife: "The one who is coming toward us has a body of divine flesh." His wife answered the scorpion-man: "Two parts of him are like a god, and only one part is human." The scorpion-man replied to her: "One of the gods has given the order. He has traveled far-off roads to reach me. The mountains he has crossed are steep."
He marches one mile, and the darkness is thick; no light comes. He marches two miles, and the darkness is thick; no light comes.

As soon as he saw it, he ran toward it. It bore jewels for fruit, and its branches hung down, beautiful to see. The branches were made of crystal, and the tree was loaded with fruit that dazzled the hero's eye.

chapters.title: Tablet X
paragraphs: The divine maiden Sabitu sat on the throne of the sea. Sabitu sees him from far off, and she speaks to herself and takes counsel with herself: "Because of this — how will he succeed in his undertaking?"

As Sabitu sees him coming, she shuts her ocean palace. She closes its gate and bars it again and again. Gilgamesh listens, and he lifts his finger. Then Gilgamesh spoke to Sabitu: "Sabitu, why do you stare at me? Why do you bolt your gate against me? I will break your gate."

And Gilgamesh said to Sabitu: "Tell me, Sabitu, which way leads to Per-napishtim? What direction does it take? Tell me its direction, Sabitu. If I can, I will cross the sea. If I cannot, I will run across the open country."

Sabitu answered Gilgamesh: "Gilgamesh, no ferry has ever run here, and no one since the earliest days has crossed this sea. Shamash the hero crosses it, but apart from Shamash, who can? The crossing is hard and the road is full of peril, and the Waters of Death lie across its mouth like a bolt. Gilgamesh, how will you cross the sea? And if you reach the Waters of Death, what will you do?

But Gilgamesh, there is Arad-Ea, the boatman of Per-napishtim, who works beside the stone ones; in the forest he cuts down a cedar. Let your eyes find him. If it is possible, cross over with him. If it is not possible, turn back." When Gilgamesh heard this, he lifted the axe at his side, drew the sword from his belt, slipped in and went down, and fell like a javelin among them.

Arad-Ea said to Gilgamesh: "Your own hand, Gilgamesh, has blocked the crossing. You have smashed the stone ones. They are smashed now, and the rest is gone. Take the axe at your side, Gilgamesh, go into the wood, and make one hundred and twenty oars, each five gar long."

When Gilgamesh heard this, he took the axe at his side and drew the sword from his belt. He went into the woods and cut down trees for one hundred and twenty oars, five gar long each, coated them with pitch, and brought them to Arad-Ea. Then Gilgamesh and Arad-Ea boarded the boat, and it tossed back and forth as they went. They covered a journey of forty-five days in three days, and so Arad-Ea reached the Waters of Death.

Per-napishtim, watching him from far off, began to think, and he reasoned with himself: "Why are the stone ones of the ship smashed? And someone who is not one of mine rides in the ship. Is the one who comes there not a man? Does he not have the right side of a man? I look: is that not a human being? I look: is that not a man? I look: is that not a god? He is like me in every way."

"The friend I loved has turned to clay, my friend Enkidu. I will not lie down like him, and I will not sink to where my friend lies now." Then Gilgamesh said to Per-napishtim: "Here I am. I have come to see Per-napishtim, whom people call the Distant One. I will turn to him for help. I have passed through every land, crossed the steep mountains, and sailed over every sea."

For as long as houses are raised, for as long as contracts are sealed, for as long as brothers feud, for as long as hatred and conflict remain in the land, for as long as rivers carry their floods to the sea, there is never a likeness of death drawn. When the alu-demon and the eziz-demon meet a man, the Anunnaki, the great gods, assemble, and the goddess of fate, who decides fates alongside them, will act, for they appoint death and life. But the days of death are not made known to mankind.

chapters.title: Tablet XI
paragraphs: Gilgamesh said to Per-napishtim, the Distant One: "I look at you in amazement, Per-napishtim! Your appearance has not changed; you are just like me. Your very nature has not changed; you are just like me, though you have left this life. But my heart still has to struggle against everything that no longer weighs on you. Tell me how you came to live here and win eternal life among the gods."

Per-napishtim then said to Gilgamesh: "I will uncover for you, Gilgamesh, a hidden tale, and I will tell you what the gods kept secret. You know the city of Shurippak, which sits on the bank of the Euphrates. That city had become corrupt, so the gods inside it, the great gods, resolved to send a deluge. Their father Anu was there, and their counselor, the warrior Bel, and their leader Ninib, and their champion En-nu-gi. But Ea, lord of unfathomable wisdom, argued with them, and what they planned he told to a reed hut: 'Reed hut, reed hut, clay wall, clay wall! Listen, reed hut; pay attention, clay wall!

Man of Shurippak, son of Ubara-Tutu, tear down your house and build a ship. Give up your possessions and look to your life! Abandon your goods and save your life, and bring living seed of every kind into the ship. The ship you will build must have carefully measured proportions: let its breadth and its length match each other, and then launch it into the sea.' I paid attention and said to Ea, my lord: 'My lord, I will do as you have commanded. I will watch and carry out the order. But what shall I tell the city, the people, and the elders?'

Ea opened his mouth and spoke, and he said to me, his servant: 'Man, give them this answer: "I know that Bel hates me. I cannot go on living in your city, nor can I safely stay on Bel's ground any longer. I will go down to the deep and make my home with Ea, my lord. For a time he will shower rich blessings on you: birds in plenty and fish in great numbers, cattle in herds and a rich harvest. Shamash has fixed the hour when the rulers of darkness will rain destruction down upon you in the evening."'
As soon as early dawn appeared, I feared the brightness of the day, and I gathered together everything that was needed.

On the fifth day I laid out its plan. Its walls stood ten gar high at the middle, and its deck measured ten gar across. I added a roof at the front and closed it in. I built six stories, which made seven levels in all, and divided the inside of each level into nine rooms. I cut out spouts for water inside. I chose a pole and added all the necessary fittings. I smeared three shar of pitch on the outside, and for the inside, to make it watertight, I used three shar of asphalt. The men hauled three shar of oil in baskets. I set one shar of oil aside for sacrifices, and the boatman stowed the other two.

I slaughtered oxen for the temple of the gods, and killed lambs day after day. I poured out jugs of cider, oil, and sweet wine, and large bowls of them like river water, as libations. I held a feast like the feast of New Year's Day. My hands brought oil to the god Shamash. Then the ship was finished.

The work was heavy. I fitted rigging above and below, and when it was all finished, the ship sat in the water two thirds of its depth. I loaded it with everything I owned. I loaded it with all my silver, with all my gold, and with living creatures of every kind. Then I brought on board my whole family and my kin, the cattle and wild animals of the field, and the righteous people. All of them I brought aboard.

Shamash had set a time: 'When the rulers of darkness send a ruinous rain in the evening, board the ship and shut the door.' That very sign arrived: in the evening the rulers of darkness sent a ruinous rain. I watched the storm come on and was too frightened to look at it. I boarded the ship and shut the door. I put the great house and all that it held in the care of the boatman Purur-bel.

As morning broke, a black cloud climbed up from the horizon. Within it the weather god Adad thundered, and Nabu and the king of the gods, Marduk, marched in front. The destroyers swept across mountain and plain. The great Dibbara wrenched the anchor cable loose. Ninib came forward and made the banks burst. The Anunnaki raised their torches and lit up the whole world with their glare. The storm Adad had brought rose all the way to the heavens, and every ray of light turned to darkness. It flooded the land. It blew with violence, and in a single day it climbed above the mountains. Like an assault in battle it rushed upon the people. Brother could not look out for brother, and from the sky no one could be told apart. The gods themselves feared the storm. They fled and took refuge in the heaven of Anu, and there they cowered like dogs, crouching along the barrier of heaven.

Then Ishtar screamed like a woman in labor, and the lady of the gods lamented in a loud voice: 'The world of long ago has turned back to clay, because I spoke in favor of this evil in the gods' assembly. Alas, that I spoke for this evil in the council of the gods and argued for the destruction of my own people! What I brought forth, where is it? Like the spawn of fish it fills the sea.' The gods mourned the Anunnaki along with her. Bowed low, they sat weeping, lips pressed shut in fear and terror.

For six days and nights the wind blew, and storm and tempest overran the land. When the seventh day arrived, the tempest, the storm, the battle they had fought like a mighty army, began to ease. The sea settled, and the hurricane and storm stopped. I looked out across the sea and cried out, but all of humanity had turned to clay. The riverbeds lay flat like the fields around them. I opened the hatch, and daylight fell on my face. Stunned, I sank back and sat weeping, with tears streaming down my face. I looked in every direction, and everything was sea.

After twelve days a strip of land appeared above the water. The ship drifted toward Mount Nisir, and there on Mount Nisir the boat stuck fast and could not slip away. For the first day and the second, Mount Nisir held the ship and would not let it move. For the third day and the fourth, Mount Nisir held the ship and would not let it move. For the fifth day and the sixth, Mount Nisir held the ship and would not let it move. As the seventh day approached, I sent out a dove and released her. The dove flew about, but she found nowhere to rest and came back. Then I sent out a swallow and released her. The swallow flew about, but she found nowhere to rest and came back as well. Then I sent out a raven and released her. The raven flew off and saw the waters draining away. She settled to feed, wandered off, and never came back.

Then I let everything out toward the four winds and offered a sacrifice. I poured out a libation on the peak of the mountain. I set out incense burners, seven and seven, and put in them calamus, cedar wood, and sweet incense. The gods smelled the scent; yes, the gods smelled the sweet scent, and they gathered like flies around the one who offered it.

But when the lady of the gods, Ishtar, drew near, she held up the great jewels that Anu had made at her wish and said: 'Gods who are here! By the necklace I wear, I swear it: these days I will keep in mind, and I will never forget them. Let the gods come to the offering, but let Bel stay away from it, since he recklessly caused the flood and gave my people over to destruction.'

When Bel came near and saw the ship, the god was seized with fury. Rage against the gods, the Igigi, filled his heart, and he said: 'Who has come through alive? No man was supposed to survive the destruction.' Then Ninib spoke up and said to Bel, the warrior: 'Who could have devised this but Ea! Does Ea not know every craft?'

Then Ea opened his mouth and spoke to Bel, the warrior: 'You wisest of the gods, you warrior, how rash of you to bring on a flood-storm! Let the sinner bear his sin and the wicked man his wickedness, but be merciful and hold back, and do not let everything be destroyed! Be considerate, and do not let everything be thrown into chaos! Instead of sending a flood-storm, let lions come and thin out mankind. Instead of sending a flood-storm, let tigers come and thin out mankind. Instead of sending a flood-storm, let famine come and strike the land. Instead of sending a flood-storm, let plague come and kill off the people. I did not reveal the secret of the great gods. Someone made Atrachasis see it in a dream, and that is how he learned the secret of the gods.'

Then Bel reached a decision. He went up into the ship, took me by the hand, and brought me out. He brought out my wife too and made her kneel at my side. He turned us toward each other and stood between us and blessed us: 'Up to now Per-napishtim has been a mere mortal. From now on Per-napishtim and his wife will be as high as the gods. Per-napishtim will dwell far away, where the rivers meet.' Then they carried us off and settled us far away at the mouth of the rivers.

"As for you, which of the gods can grant you the power to win the life you long for? Now sleep!" Gilgamesh lay helpless for six days and seven nights, like a lame man. Sleep swept over him like a storm wind. Then Per-napishtim said to his wife: "Look at the hero who longs for life! Sleep has swept over him like a storm wind." His wife replied to Per-napishtim, the Distant One: "Touch him with change. Let the man eat the charm-root. Let him go back in good health along the road he came by, and let him leave through the great gate for his own land."

Per-napishtim said to his wife: "The man's suffering and torment trouble you. Well then, cook his food now and put it at his head." While Gilgamesh slept on board his ship, she cooked the food and set it at his head. While he slept on board his ship, first his food was prepared; second, it was peeled; third, it was moistened; fourth, it was cleaned; fifth, shiba, which means old age, was added; sixth, it was cooked; and seventh, suddenly the man was transformed, having eaten the magic food.

Then Gilgamesh spoke to Per-napishtim, the Distant One: "I had sunk down, and sleep had overcome me. Suddenly you charmed me, and so you helped me." And Per-napishtim said to Gilgamesh: "Gilgamesh, take some of your food. What will be told to you is this: first, your food was prepared; second, it was peeled; third, it was moistened; fourth, it was cleaned; fifth, shipa was added; sixth, it was cooked; and seventh, I suddenly transformed you, and you ate the magic food."

And Gilgamesh said to Per-napishtim, the Distant One: "What shall I do, Per-napishtim? Where shall I go? The demon of the dead has seized my friend. Death now sits on my couch. And wherever I turn, there is death."

And Per-napishtim said to Arad-Ea, the ferryman: "Arad-Ea, let the boat take you, and keep out anyone who tries to board the ship. The man you are leading has sores all over his body, and the rash on his skin has spoiled the beauty of his body. Take him, Arad-Ea, to the place of cleansing, where he can wash his sores in water until they are white as snow. Let him shed his diseased skin and let the sea carry it off. His body will look healthy again. Set a turban on his head once more, and clothe his nakedness. Until he reaches his city, until he arrives at his road, the garment must not wear out; it must stay perfectly new."

Arad-Ea took him to the place of purification, where he washed his sores in water until they were white as snow. He threw off his sore-covered skin and the sea carried it away. His body looked healthy again. He put the turban back on his head, and the garment to cover his nakedness, until he should return to his city and reach his road. The garment did not wear thin; it stayed completely new. Then Gilgamesh and Arad-Ea set out in the boat again, and during their journey it tossed back and forth.

The wife of Per-napishtim spoke to her husband, the Distant One: "Gilgamesh went away, worked hard, and pulled the oar. What will you give him to take back to his land?" Gilgamesh raised the pole and pulled the boat in toward the shore. Then Per-napishtim spoke to Gilgamesh: "Gilgamesh, you went away, worked hard, and pulled the oar. What can I give you to carry you back to your land? I will disclose to you, Gilgamesh, a secret, and I will announce to you what the gods have decided. A certain plant looks like buckthorn, and it stings with its thorn like a bramble. When your hands can reach that plant —"

When Gilgamesh heard this, he opened the way and fastened heavy stones to his feet, and they pulled him down into the sea, and there he found the plant. He seized the magic plant. He cut the heavy stones from his feet; one fell away, and the second he threw down after the first. Then Gilgamesh said to Arad-Ea, the ferryman: "Arad-Ea, this plant is famous, and with it a man gets whatever his heart desires. I will carry it to mighty-walled Erech and tend it there and then cut it back. Its name is 'The old man becomes young again!' I will eat from it and go back to the vigor of my youth."

At every twenty double leagues they ate a meal, and at every thirty they rested. Gilgamesh noticed a well of cool, refreshing water. He stepped into it and drew out some water. A serpent shot out, and the plant slipped from his hands. The serpent came up out of the well and carried the plant off, and as it turned away it spat out a curse. After that Gilgamesh sat down and wept. Tears streamed over his cheeks, and he said to Arad-Ea, the ferryman:

"Why, Arad-Ea, did my hands tremble? Why did the blood of my heart stand still? I did not do myself any good. The benefit has gone to the lion of the ground. After a journey of only twenty double leagues the plant has been snatched away, as I opened the well and lowered the vessel. I see the sign; it has become an omen for me. I am to go back, leaving the ship on the shore."

They went on, eating a meal at every twenty double leagues and resting at every thirty, until they reached mighty-walled Erech. There Gilgamesh said to Arad-Ea, the ferryman: "Arad-Ea, go up and walk along the wall of Erech. Look at the foundation stone and study the brickwork. Is the wall not built of baked brick, and was its foundation not laid in pitch? 'Sevenfold is your name.'"

chapters.title: Tablet XII
paragraphs: "You go to the temple no more. You put on white garments no more. Like an ordinary mortal you have fallen. You no longer rub yourself with sweet-smelling bull's fat, and people no longer gather around you for its fragrance. You no longer bend the bow to the ground, and those slain by the bow now lie around you. You no longer carry the staff in your hand, for the spirits of death have taken you captive. You no longer tie sandals to your feet. You no longer shout a war cry here on earth.

You no longer kiss the wife you loved. You no longer strike the wife you hated. You no longer kiss the son you loved. You no longer strike the son you hated. The woes of the netherworld have overtaken you, and she who is dark has taken you, she who is dark, mother Nin-azu, who is dark, whose white, shining body is not clothed in any garment, whose breast is like the lid of a box."

"He no longer kisses the wife he loved. He no longer strikes the wife he hated. He no longer kisses the son he loved. He no longer strikes the son he hated. The woes of the earth have snatched him away, and she who is dark has taken him, she who is dark, mother Nin-azu, who is dark, whose white, shining body is not clothed in any garment, whose breast is like the lid of a box. Enkidu has gone down from the earth into darkness. Plague has not snatched him away, and wasting sickness has not snatched him away. The earth has snatched him away. The lurking demon of Nergal, the merciless, has not snatched him away. The earth has snatched him away. The battlefield has not killed him. The earth has snatched him away." Ningul wept for his servant Enkidu.

Then Gilgamesh went alone to E-kur, the temple of Bel, and prayed: "Father Bel, the sting of a fly has thrown me down on the ground. Insects have brought me low to the ground. Enkidu has sunk down to the shades. Plague has not snatched him away, and so on. The lurking demon of Nergal, the merciless, has not snatched him away. The battlefield has not killed him."

"Father Sin, the sting of a fly has thrown me down on the ground. Insects have brought me low to the ground. Enkidu has sunk down to the shades. Plague has not snatched him away, and so on. The lurking demon of Nergal, the merciless, has not snatched him away."

"Open the tomb chamber and break the earth, that the spirit of Enkidu may climb out of the ground like a wind." When Nergal, the hero and lord, heard this prayer, he broke open the chamber of the tomb and split the ground, and he made the spirit of Enkidu rise out of the earth like a wind.

"Tell me, my friend, oh tell me, my friend, how the country looks that you have seen. Oh, tell me!" But Enkidu answered: "I cannot tell you, my friend, I cannot tell you. If I described to you how the country I have seen looks, you would sit down and cry."

Gilgamesh said to him: "Then let me sit down and weep! Everything that once gladdened your heart is bitter and sad. All of it is there, like an old garment that the worm eats. What you did in this life, what once gladdened your heart, is all cloaked in dust."

The one who rests on a soft couch and drinks pure water is the hero slain in battle, you and I have often seen such a man: his father and mother hold up his head, and his wife kneels at his side. Yes! the spirit of such a man is at rest. But the man whose corpse lies unburied in the field, you and I have often seen such a man, his spirit finds no rest in the earth. The man whose spirit has no one to care for it, you and I have often seen such a man, eats the dregs of the bowl and the broken scraps of food that are thrown out into the street."
